short: ZIC1 to ZIC5 are five-fingered C2H2 zinc-finger proteins whose DNA-binding domains are the closest relatives of GLI outside the GLIS subfamily, and which read a GLI-like site. In vitro selection gives an optimal ZIC site almost identical to the GLI consensus but bound with lower affinity; modern high-throughput measurements extend it to GACCCCCCGCTGTG, whose reverse complement, CACAGCAGGGGGT, is how several databases write the same motif. ZIC proteins also bind GLI zinc fingers directly and can raise or lower GLI-dependent transcription. They act mainly in dorsal neural tube, neural crest, somites and cerebellum, and human mutations cause holoprosencephaly (ZIC2), X-linked heterotaxy (ZIC3) and Dandy-Walker malformation (ZIC1 with ZIC4).
long:
## The factors

The ZIC family has five human members, ZIC1 to ZIC5, each with a tandem array of C2H2 zinc fingers
that is more similar to the GLI fingers than to any other vertebrate zinc-finger class. ZIC1 and
ZIC4 are a divergently transcribed pair on chromosome 3q24; ZIC2 and ZIC5 are a similar pair on
13q32; ZIC3 sits alone on Xq26 [PMID:23443491]. They bind as monomers. In addition to binding DNA, ZIC proteins
associate physically with GLI zinc fingers and, depending on cell type, either enhance or suppress
GLI-dependent transactivation [PMID:11238441,11053430], so part of their activity is exerted as a GLI cofactor rather than
through their own site. Expression is largely neural and paraxial: dorsal neural tube and roof
plate, neural crest, somites, and, postnatally, cerebellar granule cells. ZIC2 is also expressed in
early epiblast and embryonic stem cells.

## The motif

The first systematic definition of the ZIC site used gel-shift-based target selection with ZIC1,
ZIC2 and ZIC3 and recovered a sequence almost identical to the GLI binding sequence, but bound with
lower affinity than GLI [PMID:11053430]; consistently, reporter activation by ZIC proteins depended less on the
presence of a GLI site than GLI1 activation did, and ZIC proteins activated many promoters lacking
one [PMID:11053430]. Circular-dichroism comparisons of ZIC, GLI and GLIS finger domains on DNA support a shared
recognition mode [PMID:18298960].

High-throughput SELEX extends the site to a 13-14 base element usually written GACCCCCCGCTGTG [PMID:23332764]. Its
5' half, GACCCCCC, is the GLIS-like version of the GLI core, and the 3' extension GCTGTG is what
distinguishes ZIC from GLI and GLIS in practice. Several databases write the same element on the
other strand, as CACAGCAGGGGGT or the shorter CNCAGCAGG, and the ontology form CCTGCTGNG is the
reverse complement of that short core; none of these is a different motif. The data consensus here,
CNCAGCAGGGGGCC, is the reverse-strand form of the full site. One real subtlety is visible in the
collection: the HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX versions of the ZIC motif differ at a central CpG
(CAGCGGGGGG versus CAGCAGGGGG), so cytosine methylation shifts the measured preference at that
position [PMID:28473536], and different database entries for the same protein can look inconsistent for that reason.
No experiment distinguishes ZIC1 from ZIC2, ZIC3, ZIC4 or ZIC5 by sequence; the JASPAR
Zic1::Zic2 entry is modeled as a dimer but its consensus is the same short core.

## Where it acts

ZIC sites are enhancer elements. In mouse embryonic stem cells ZIC2 occupies thousands of
enhancers, both active and poised, and works with the Mbd3/NuRD chromatin-remodeling complex to regulate
genes linked to differentiation [PMID:25699711]; later work describes ZIC2 acting first as a priming factor on closed chromatin during
neural induction and then as an activator at established enhancers [PMID:42033229]. In the cerebellum and dorsal
neural tube ZIC occupancy overlaps with GLI-responsive elements, which is expected given the shared
core, and ZIC and GLI compete or cooperate at the same sequences. Because the informative part of
the site is roughly nine to thirteen bases with a GC-rich core, matches are common in GC-rich
regulatory DNA, and the motif overlaps in scoring space with GLI, GLIS and, at the CAGCAGG core,
with simple CAG-repeat and E-box-adjacent sequence.

## Biology and disease

Gli/Zic factors together pattern the vertebrate neural plate by defining domains of differentiation,
with ZIC activity dorsal to the SHH-dependent ventral domains [PMID:9634234]. Heterozygous ZIC2 loss-of-function
causes holoprosencephaly type 5, characteristically with a middle-interhemispheric variant and
distinctive facial features [PMID:29442327]; ZIC3 mutations cause X-linked heterotaxy with complex congenital heart
defects and laterality reversal [PMID:29442328]; heterozygous deletion of the linked ZIC1 and ZIC4 pair causes
Dandy-Walker malformation [PMID:15338008], and mouse work shows that combined Zic1 and Zic4 loss disturbs several
developmental programs in the cerebellar anlage rather than one [PMID:21307096]. ZIC5 was identified in Xenopus as a
neural-crest regulator [PMID:23443491]. Beyond development, ZIC family members are recurrently deregulated in
tumors, most consistently by promoter hypermethylation and silencing; ZIC1, for example, is
downregulated by promoter hypermethylation in gastric cancer [PMID:19135984].

## Reading a hit

Treat a ZIC match as "ZIC family", never as a specific paralogue: all five members share one motif.
Then treat it cautiously as "ZIC rather than GLI". The two families were defined on essentially the
same 5' core, and separating them depends on the 3' GCTGTG extension, which carries relatively
little information; a short or weak match can belong to either, and a ZIC hit inside a
Hedgehog-responsive enhancer is as likely to be a GLI site. Note also that a real ZIC effect need
not require a ZIC site at all, since ZIC proteins act as GLI cofactors and in reporter assays
activate promoters lacking the site. The GC-rich core makes the motif frequent in GC-rich
regulatory DNA, so isolated matches are weak evidence. In the data behind this family, one Vierstra
archetype labelled ZIC (AC0536) has the consensus GACCACCC and matches the GLI family better than
its own; that is the expected failure mode for this pair, not a claim that the label is wrong.
caveats: The five ZIC paralogues are indistinguishable by sequence, so a hit names the family only. The larger problem is the GLI boundary: ZIC and GLI were defined on nearly the same core, ZIC binds the GLI consensus in vitro (with lower affinity), and the two are separated only by a weakly informative 3' extension, so weak matches cannot be assigned to one family. One Vierstra archetype labelled ZIC in these data in fact scores closest to GLI. In vitro entries for the same ZIC protein can also disagree at a central CpG because the methyl-SELEX and standard SELEX preferences differ there. Finally, ZIC can act on GLI-dependent transcription without occupying its own site.

timeline.finding: zic is cloned from mouse cerebellum as a zinc-finger gene expressed in granule-cell precursors, naming the family and placing its zinc fingers closest to the GLI fingers.
timeline.open: No binding site had been measured; the GLI similarity was a sequence inference.

timeline.finding: Zic2 and Gli proteins are shown to pattern the frog neural plate into alternating domains, Zic2 inducing neural crest and inhibiting neurogenesis while Gli does the opposite, establishing the two as a functionally paired system.
timeline.open: Whether the antagonism was exerted through shared DNA sites or through protein interaction.

timeline.finding: Gel-shift target selection gives ZIC1, ZIC2 and ZIC3 a site almost identical to the GLI site but bound with lower affinity, and ZIC and GLI proteins are shown to associate physically through their zinc-finger domains and to modulate each other's activity.
timeline.methods: EMSA-based site selection with mutational analysis, reporter assays, co-immunoprecipitation
timeline.open: Because ZIC proteins also activated promoters lacking the site, how much of their activity is site-dependent was unclear.

timeline.finding: Heterozygous deletion of the linked ZIC1-ZIC4 pair is identified as a cause of Dandy-Walker malformation, giving the family its first human cerebellar phenotype.
timeline.methods: Human deletion mapping in patients, mouse expression analysis

timeline.finding: HT-SELEX extends the ZIC site to a 13-14 base element, GACCCCCCGCTGTG, whose 3' GCTGTG extension is what separates it from the GLI and GLIS versions of the shared GC-rich core.
timeline.open: Whether the low-information 3' extension is used to partition sites in vivo.

timeline.finding: ZIC2 is mapped genome-wide in mouse embryonic stem cells and found at thousands of enhancers, where it is required for normal differentiation, moving the family from a patterning gene to a measured enhancer-binding factor.
timeline.methods: ChIP-seq, proteomics of associated complexes, differentiation assays

timeline.finding: Methyl-HT-SELEX shows that the measured ZIC preference shifts at the central CpG, so the HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX models of the same protein differ (CAGCGGGGGG versus CAGCAGGGGG).
timeline.open: Whether methylation-dependent ZIC binding occurs at methylated regulatory DNA in cells.

timeline.finding: During neural induction from mouse embryonic stem cells, ZIC2 binds de novo to closed distal enhancers and raises their accessibility at pluripotency exit, then activates a subset of those primed enhancers, so one factor occupies the same sites in two mechanistically different roles; ZIC3 compensates for its loss in the pluripotent state.
timeline.methods: Genome editing in mESC-derived neural progenitors, ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, transcriptomics
timeline.open: What converts a primed ZIC2-bound enhancer into an active one is not identified.

open: How much of ZIC activity runs through the ZIC site itself is unsettled: ZIC proteins activate reporters lacking the site and bind GLI zinc fingers directly, yet genome-wide maps show them occupying thousands of enhancers in a sequence-dependent way.

Whether the 3' GCTGTG extension is actually used in cells to partition sites between ZIC and GLI/GLIS is unknown; it is the only feature separating the two families in vitro, and it carries little information.

Whether the methylation-dependent shift at the central CpG, seen when HT-SELEX and methyl-HT-SELEX models of the same ZIC protein are compared, has any counterpart at methylated enhancers in vivo has not been tested.

Nothing in the measured specificities separates ZIC1 from ZIC2, ZIC3, ZIC4 or ZIC5, yet their loss-of-function phenotypes differ sharply (holoprosencephaly, heterotaxy, Dandy-Walker malformation); whether that reflects expression domains alone or unmeasured differences in site preference or partner use is open.
